slides.heading: How Quantum Computing Works
slides.body: The technology that could change everything we know about computation

slides.heading: Classical vs. Quantum Bits
slides.body: A classical computer uses bits — either 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits, which can be 0, 1, or both at the same time thanks to a property called superposition. This allows quantum computers to explore many solutions simultaneously.

slides.heading: Superposition: Being Two Things At Once
slides.body: Superposition lets a qubit exist in multiple states until it is measured. Imagine spinning a coin — while it spins, it's neither heads nor tails. Only when it lands does it become one. Qubits behave similarly until observed.

slides.heading: Entanglement: Spooky Action
slides.body: Entanglement links two qubits so that the state of one instantly determines the state of the other, no matter the distance. Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance.' This lets quantum computers coordinate information without classical communication.

slides.heading: Interference: Amplifying Right Answers
slides.body: Quantum algorithms use interference to cancel out wrong paths and amplify correct solutions — similar to how noise-canceling headphones work with sound waves. This steers the computation toward the right answer efficiently.

slides.heading: Why Temperature Matters
slides.body: Qubits are extremely fragile. Most quantum computers must operate near absolute zero (−273°C) — colder than outer space — to prevent thermal noise from disrupting quantum states. Maintaining this environment is one of engineering's hardest challenges.

slides.heading: What Quantum Computers Are Good At
slides.body: Quantum computers excel at specific problems: simulating molecules for drug discovery, optimizing complex logistics, breaking and creating encryption, and training certain AI models. They don't replace classical computers — they complement them.

slides.heading: Quantum vs. Classical: The Race
slides.body: Google's quantum processor solved in 200 seconds a problem that would take a classical supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM, Microsoft, and startups are racing to build more stable, scalable quantum systems with practical real-world applications.

slides.heading: The Threat to Encryption
slides.body: Today's encryption relies on math problems too hard for classical computers. A powerful quantum computer could crack them in minutes. Governments and tech companies are already developing 'post-quantum cryptography' to protect future data.

slides.heading: The Quantum Future
slides.body: Quantum computing is still in its early days, but its potential is enormous. From curing diseases to securing the internet, understanding this technology today means being ready for a radically different computational world tomorrow.
